How to play
  1. Tap a city on the map to travel. Persuade the musicians in each city to join your orchestra.
  2. A persuasion lasts 8 bars. Use Fee, Scandal, Theory, Fame and Passion as the moment requires; push the rapport needle all the way to the right and they are won over. Different approaches work on different people (and repeating one weakens it).
  3. When inspiration is full, a cadenza gives a big push. Attend a salon beforehand and you start with inspiration already stored.
  4. If talks break down, you can convince them in a performance duel: Technique, Expression and Improvisation, like rock-paper-scissors.
  5. Persuade the ruler of a city (a theatre or a court) and the city is yours, with an income every month.
  6. Every month the rival camps poach musicians, seize cities and launch concert wars against your cities. Win back their cities by concert war and their followers by poaching.
  7. Those far above you (Lv more than your fame Lv+2) will turn you away. Give concerts to raise your fame.
  8. Choose a venue: salon, medium hall or large theatre. Bigger earns more but empties more easily. The audience's reaction (bravos, bouquets, swoons, boos, dozing, walk-outs) depends on the reception.
  9. Each player has a ★trait (attendance +20%, strings +3, lesson income…) and a quirk (frail, miser, difficult, amorous…). When satisfaction falls they may leave, or go over to a rival. A friend already in your orchestra will put in a word during persuasion.
  10. Scouting: first 🔍scout (150 fr) to learn which approaches work, the growth type (early / normal / late), potential, contract terms and chemistry. Without scouting you cannot tell which approach worked. Once they are won over, negotiate the signing fee and salary (haggling is a gamble).
  11. Ensemble and chemistry: the more two players appear together, the higher their ensemble Lv and the better the reception. Pairs with ◎○ chemistry grow quickly; ✕ pairs drag each other down and lose satisfaction.
  12. Growth types: early bloomers grow fast at first but decline from the fifth year; late bloomers grow strongly after two and a half years.
  13. Meet the victory conditions and you face the final showdown (best of three). Win it and the grand concert follows.
  14. At a concert you choose the programme and place your players in each part, like a football formation. The abilities the piece calls for, form (which changes monthly), historical partnerships (chemistry), the composer's presence and the city's taste decide the reception (★).
  15. In a performance duel, taking a player as your second strengthens that person's best card.
  16. There are five difficulty levels: Beginner, Normal, Hard, Very hard, Inferno. The victory conditions (cities held and seats filled) and the time limit vary with difficulty. The more cities you hold, the more wary the remaining theatres and courts become, and their rank rises.
  17. Fame tops out at Lv30. After clearing the game you can go on without a time limit in endless mode and collect 🏅achievements.

In June you were thrown out by Count Arco, chamberlain to the Archbishop of Salzburg — literally with a kick on the backside.

You give up the post of court musician to live in Vienna as a freelance.
History: with this 'kick' Mozart broke with the court of Salzburg.
The ladies of the Warsaw salons
The organ of St James's is where I belong.
An organist and friar of Prague, called 'the Bohemian Bach'. He is also said to have taught Tartini and Gluck.
The singing I learned in Italy, for the chants of Russia.
The court chapel choir and I are at your service.
Born in Ukraine. After studying in Italy he returned to St Petersburg in 1779 and led the court chapel choir.
In playing folk songs I yield to no one.
I long to play freely, away from the court.
One of Russia's earliest violin virtuosos, known for his variations on Russian folk songs.
I was born on a Bohemian farm.
Born in Bohemia. He wrote many symphonies in Vienna and is said to have played string quartets with Haydn and Mozart.
Teaching the young ladies of Vienna is my best income.
The sound of fashion, for your orchestra.
A Bohemian-born pianist and composer. He moved to Vienna in 1778 and also taught the piano to the imperial family.
Prague is a city that loves music.
My wife Josepha and I are at your service.
A pianist of Prague. He later welcomed Mozart to the Villa Bertramka outside the city and watched over the finishing of Don Giovanni.
That boy overturned everything I taught him.
The heart of Poland, for your orchestra.
Director of the Warsaw Conservatory and Chopin's teacher. On Chopin's report he wrote: 'musical genius'.
The lights of the National Theatre must not go out.
A baton trained in the theatre, for your orchestra.
Conductor of the National Theatre in Warsaw. From the podium he supported the young Chopin's Warsaw concerts.
I have stood on the same stage as Paganini.
The Polish bow, in your orchestra.
A Polish violin virtuoso. He played a double concerto with Paganini, who is said to have rated him 'the second best'.
I have grown used even to the Moscow winter.
An Irish-born pianist who lived in Moscow. He created the form of the 'nocturne' and influenced Chopin.
I am the one who keeps the Moscow theatres running.
Opera in Russian, with your orchestra.
A composer who ran the theatres of Moscow. His opera Askold's Grave was a great hit.
Russian imperial anthem 'God Save the Tsar!' (1833)
My duties at court keep me busy.
The sound of the Russian court, for your orchestra.
A violin virtuoso and an army officer. In 1833 he composed the anthem of the Russian Empire.
I have been teaching in Prague for decades now.
A great teacher of Prague. His piano 'eclogues' are sometimes called forerunners of Schubert's impromptus.
I have come this far following in Paganini's footsteps.
From Brno in Moravia. He followed Paganini about, stole his secrets, and was called his successor.
My piano and my baton, for your orchestra.
Founder of the Moscow Conservatory. At first he tore Tchaikovsky's First Piano Concerto to pieces; later he played it himself.
I have not finished my counterpoint homework yet.
My teacher's concerto, with your orchestra.
The young pianist who played his teacher Tchaikovsky's First Piano Concerto in Moscow in 1875.
The piano is there to be made to sing.
The Russian lion will join your orchestra.
Founder of the St Petersburg Conservatory. A great pianist said to resemble Beethoven in both looks and playing.
In the navy I read charts rather than scores.
A former naval officer. He taught at the St Petersburg Conservatory from 1871, and is said to have relearned harmony as he taught it.
…I should like to give up my post in the civil service.
The truth of Russia, for your orchestra.
One of the 'Mighty Handful' (The Five). He wrote Boris Godunov and Pictures at an Exhibition while working as a civil servant.
Symphonic poem: In the Steppes of Central Asia
I write a little at a time, between experiments.
A head for chemistry and a head for music, both for your orchestra.
A chemist and medical-school professor by profession. He kept composing as, in his own words, a 'Sunday composer'.
